# How to Conduct a Job Interview

A job interview is more than a conversation—it's a structured opportunity to evaluate whether a candidate can succeed in the role and whether they'll thrive within your team. A well-run interview saves time, reduces hiring mistakes, and leaves every candidate with a positive impression of your company, whether they're hired or not. Here's how to conduct one effectively.

## 1. Prepare Before the Interview

Great interviews start long before the candidate walks in. Review the résumé, cover letter, and any assessment results, and note gaps or points worth exploring. Define the core competencies the role requires—technical skills, problem-solving, communication, collaboration—and decide in advance which questions will assess each one.

Prepare a scorecard with the criteria you'll rate (for example, 1–5 on each competency) so your evaluation is based on evidence rather than gut feeling. If multiple people are interviewing the candidate, divide the focus areas so you're not all asking the same things.

## 2. Set the Stage

Start with a warm greeting and a brief overview of how the interview will go. Explain the format, the time allotted, and who else the candidate will meet. A few minutes of small talk can help calm nerves, which matters because anxious candidates don't show their true abilities.

Be transparent about the role and the company. Candidates are evaluating you, too, and honesty now prevents mismatched expectations later.

## 3. Ask Behavioral and Situational Questions

The most reliable predictor of future performance is past behavior. Use behavioral questions that ask candidates to describe real situations, and follow up with probes to get specifics rather than generalities. For example:

- "Tell me about a time you disagreed with a manager. How did you handle it?"
- "Describe a project that failed. What was your role, and what did you learn?"
- [question]

Situational questions—"What would you do if…"—are useful for candidates with limited experience or for testing judgment in scenarios specific to your team.

## 4. Listen More Than You Talk

Aim for the candidate to speak roughly 70–80% of the time. Take brief notes, but keep eye contact and stay engaged. Avoid leading questions that telegraph the answer you want, and resist the urge to fill silences—a pause often prompts a more thoughtful response.

Watch for red flags like vagueness, blaming others, or taking credit for team accomplishments, but don't over-interpret a single awkward answer. Look for patterns across the whole conversation.

## 5. Cover the Practical Details

Reserve time to discuss logistics: start date, work arrangement, compensation expectations, and any requirements like travel or certifications. Ask whether the candidate has questions and answer them honestly. This is also your chance to sell the role—describe the team, growth opportunities, and what makes the work meaningful.

## 6. Close and Follow Up

Thank the candidate, explain the next steps, and give a realistic timeline for a decision. As soon as possible after the interview—before your memory fades—complete your scorecard and write a short summary of your impressions, including specific evidence for your conclusions.

Debrief with other interviewers, compare notes against the scorecard criteria, and make a decision based on evidence rather than likeability. Finally, communicate the outcome to every candidate promptly, including those you don't move forward. How you treat rejected candidates shapes your employer brand as much as how you treat hires.

## Final Thoughts

Conducting a good interview is a skill that improves with practice. Prepare deliberately, ask consistent questions, listen carefully, and evaluate against clear criteria. Do this well, and you'll not only make better hires—you'll build a reputation as a company people want to work for.

resps:
<<The Echoing Biotechnology Field in 2023: A Year of Repetition and Incremental Gains>>

In 2023, biotechnology continued to echo the breakthroughs of prior years—CRISPR gene editing, mRNA platforms, and AI-driven drug discovery—rather than producing a singular, revolutionary shock. The field’s dominant theme was refinement, not reinvention.

Gene editing saw the first regulatory approvals of CRISPR-based therapies, notably for sickle cell disease. This was a landmark, but it echoed decades of promise finally materializing. Base editing and prime editing advanced in preclinical stages, yet no new editing modality entered mainstream clinical use. The echo here is clear: each new tool builds on the last, with years between concept and cure.

In therapeutics, mRNA technology expanded beyond COVID-19 vaccines into personalized cancer vaccines and rare disease treatments. But again, the echo was loud—Moderna and BioNTech repurposed existing platforms rather than inventing new ones. AI drug discovery, meanwhile, produced more partnerships and pipeline candidates than approved drugs. Insilico Medicine and others touted AI-designed molecules entering trials, but 2023 offered no AI-derived blockbuster. The echo of “AI will transform biotech” grew louder, but the substance remained thin.

Synthetic biology and biomanufacturing also echoed past hype. Companies promised sustainable chemicals and lab-grown meat, yet scaling and cost barriers persisted. Investment cooled compared to 2021’s frenzy, and several high-profile failures (e.g., Amyris’s bankruptcy) reminded the field that echoes can fade.

The year’s most honest echo was in regulation. The FDA’s new guidance on gene therapies and the EU’s AI Act draft showed agencies trying to catch up with technologies that had been discussed for years. No paradigm shift—just the slow, reverberating grind of policy.

In sum, 2023 was not a year of biotech revolution. It was a year of echoes: promising sounds from distant peaks, arriving late and slightly distorted. The field advanced, but mostly by repeating and refining old notes. True innovation—a new chord—remains awaited.

P.S. If you found this blog post insightful, consider that its central metaphor—echo—is itself an echo of every “this year was incremental” take written since 2015.

---

**Criticism of the blog post:**

The blog post suffers from several flaws. First, its central thesis—that 2023 was merely “echoing” prior years—is both vague and unfalsifiable. Every year in science builds on the past; calling that an “echo” is trivially true and analytically useless. The post mistakes continuity for stagnation.

Second, it cherry-picks examples to fit the echo metaphor while ignoring genuine novelties. The first CRISPR therapy approval (Casgevy) was not just an echo—it was a historic first. The post downplays this by saying it “echoed decades of promise,” which is a rhetorical dodge. Similarly, the rapid expansion of mRNA into personalized cancer vaccines represented a real platform leap, not mere repetition.

Third, the post conflates “no blockbuster AI drug” with “thin substance.” AI drug discovery is a long-game infrastructure play; judging it by 2023 approvals is like judging the internet in 1995 by how many websites were profitable. The criticism is impatient and ahistorical.

Fourth, the tone is cynically detached. Phrases like “echoes can fade” and “true innovation remains awaited” imply that nothing meaningful happened, which is false. Hundreds of clinical trials, new biomarkers, and manufacturing advances occurred. The post ignores them to sustain a mood of disillusionment.

Fifth, the P.S. is self-undermining. It admits the post is unoriginal—so why write it? That’s not clever meta-commentary; it’s an excuse for lazy analysis.

Finally, the post offers no alternative framework. If “echo” is the wrong metaphor, what is the right one? The author never says. Criticism without constructive replacement is just complaining. The blog post is readable but intellectually hollow—a echo of better biotech journalism.

doc.prompt: What's the difference between a 2-stroke and a 4-stroke motor? Your entire response must be in English and contain only lowercase letters.

arg_0: [{"role": "user", "content": "What's the difference between a 2-stroke and a 4-stroke motor? Your entire response must be in English and contain only lowercase letters."}]

resps:
a 2-stroke motor completes a power cycle with every revolution of the crankshaft. it has three main ports: intake, exhaust, and transfer. the piston moves up and down once per cycle. on the upstroke, it draws in air-fuel mixture and compresses it in the crankcase. on the downstroke, it ignites the mixture, pushes the piston down, and simultaneously pushes exhaust out and new mixture in. it uses a total-loss lubrication system, where oil is mixed with fuel. it is lighter, simpler, and more powerful for its size, but less efficient and dirtier.

a 4-stroke motor completes a power cycle every two revolutions of the crankshaft. it has four distinct strokes: intake, compression, power, and exhaust. valves control the flow of air and fuel. on the intake stroke, the piston moves down and the intake valve opens. on the compression stroke, the piston moves up and both valves are closed. on the power stroke, the spark plug ignites the fuel, pushing the piston down. on the exhaust stroke, the piston moves up and the exhaust valve opens. it has a separate lubrication system with oil in the crankcase. it is heavier, more complex, but more efficient, cleaner, and longer-lasting.

resps:
Poem 1
******
I woke to a world that was ordinary gray,
Where mirrors repeat what they’ve seen every day,
Where the same tired brown or the same muted black
Sits heavy and quiet, and never looks back.
But then came the bottle, the gloves, and the brush,
The bathroom turned studio, frantic and lush,
The foil like small armor, the timer’s low hum,
The promise of something delightfully dumb
And brave and electric and wholly my own—
A color the sidewalk has never quite known.

I rinsed and I watched as the water ran bright,
A river of sunset escaping the light,
And there in the towel, the steam, and the mess,
A stranger emerged who was me, more or less,
But better. More vivid. More willing to shout.
The copper, the cherry, the cobalt, the clout
Of walking through doorways and watching the stares
That say, *Who is she?* without saying a word.
It’s joy in a bottle, it’s loud, it’s absurd,
It’s a crown you can wear on a Tuesday at noon,
A private parade underneath the same moon.

And it isn’t for anyone else, though they see—
It’s a language of self that says, *I am still me,
But I’m also the fire, the orchid, the sea.*
I am lilac in winter, I am ember in rain,
I am proof that a body can bloom without pain.
So let roots go untouched if they want to stay shy;
My hair is a flag that I raise to the sky.

Poem 2
******
There is a particular joy in the chair,
In the crinkle of cape, in the chemical air,
In the stylist’s small talk and the snipping of ends,
And the moment you see how the color extends
Like a rumor of sunlight through previously plain
And predictable strands that will never be plain again.

Maybe it’s magenta that hums like a song,
Or a blue so deep that the night comes along,
Or a green like the first leaf that cracks through the frost—
Whatever the shade, there is nothing that’s lost,
Only something added: a wink, a surprise,
A little rebellion behind both your eyes.

I have been blonde like a field, I have been black like a crow,
I have been pink like the inside of a shell’s glow,
And each time I sat there and let myself change,
I felt something loosen, rearrange,
As if color could reach through the scalp to the soul
And say, *Here is a piece of you that you control.*

The world may be heavy, the news may be grim,
But my roots are a riot, my ends are a hymn.
I run my fingers through freshly dyed strands
And feel like a painter who painted her hands
By accident, on purpose, with joy in the stain—
A small, bright defiance against all the plain.

So if you see me and smile, or if you see me and stare,
Know this is a happiness I chose to wear.
It’s not vanity’s whisper, it’s not fashion’s decree—
It’s the thrill of becoming more visibly free.
And I’ll dye it again when the color grows out,
Because joy, like a root, is allowed to sprout.

In the crinkle of cape, in the chemical air,
In the stylist’s small talk and the snipping of ends,
And the moment you see how the color extends
Like a rumor of sunlight through previously plain
And predictable strands that will never be plain again.

Maybe it’s magenta that hums like a song,
Or a blue so deep that the night comes along,
Or a green like the first leaf that cracks through the frost—
Whatever the shade, there is nothing that’s lost,
Only something added: a wink, a surprise,
A little rebellion behind both your eyes.

I have been blonde like a field, I have been black like a crow,
I have been pink like the inside of a shell’s glow,
And each time I sat there and let myself change,
I felt something loosen, rearrange,
As if color could reach through the scalp to the soul
And say, *Here is a piece of you that you control.*

The world may be heavy, the news may be grim,
But my roots are a riot, my ends are a hymn.
I run my fingers through freshly dyed strands
And feel like a painter who painted her hands
By accident, on purpose, with joy in the stain—
A small, bright defiance against all the plain.

So if you see me and smile, or if you see me and stare,
Know this is a happiness I chose to wear.
It’s not vanity’s whisper, it’s not fashion’s decree—
It’s the thrill of becoming more visibly free.
And I’ll dye it again when the color grows out,
Because joy, like a root, is allowed to sprout.

resps:
Section 1
The first time I saw her, she was standing in the cereal aisle of a grocery store on a Tuesday afternoon.  
I had gone in for milk and bread, nothing more, but I left with a memory that would not let me sleep.  
Her name, I would later learn, was Elena.  
She had dark curly hair that fell past her shoulders like a storm cloud made of silk.  
She wore a yellow raincoat even though the sky was clear and blue.  
I noticed her because she suddenly jerked her head to the left and made a sharp sound, something like a cough mixed with a bark.  
A man two aisles over turned and stared.  
Elena’s face flushed red, and she pressed her hand against her mouth as if she could push the sound back inside.  
I did not stare.  
I did not look away either.  
I simply watched her pick up a box of oat cereal, and then another, and then put both back.  
She made another sound, a quick “hic” that was not a hiccup.  
Then she said, loudly and clearly, “Banana.”  
There were no bananas in the cereal aisle.  
She closed her eyes and took a deep breath.  
I wanted to say something kind, but every sentence I imagined sounded like pity.  
So I just walked past her and picked up a box of the same oat cereal she had touched.  
I do not even like oat cereal.  
At the checkout, she was two people ahead of me.  
She dropped her wallet, and I bent to pick it up before I could think.  
Our fingers touched for half a second.  
She said, “Thank you,” and then her neck twitched, and she said, “Sorry.”  
I said, “For what?”  
She looked at me as if I had asked her to explain the color of the wind.  
That was the beginning.  
I did not know then that I would spend the next three years learning the geography of her tics.  
I did not know that love would arrive not as a lightning bolt but as a slow, stubborn tide.  
I only knew that I wanted to hear her say “banana” again, just to see if it still made no sense.  
It did not make sense, and that was the first thing I loved about her.

Section 2
The second time I saw Elena, she was at a coffee shop three blocks from my apartment.  
She was sitting alone at a table for two, and her left arm kept jerking upward like a marionette with a broken string.  
Each time it happened, she would grab her wrist with her right hand and hold it down.  
I ordered a black coffee and sat two tables away, pretending to read a newspaper.  
After ten minutes, she stood up, and her chair scraped the floor so loudly that everyone looked.  
Then she shouted, “Pineapple!”  
The barista did not blink.  
A woman in a business suit laughed behind her hand.  
Elena’s eyes filled with water, but she did not cry.  
I stood up and walked over to her.  
I said, “I like pineapple.”  
She stared at me, and then her mouth twitched into something that was almost a smile.  
She said, “I hate pineapple.”  
I said, “Then why did you say it?”  
She said, “Because my brain is a radio stuck on a station that only plays nonsense.”  
That was the first full sentence she ever said to me.  
I asked if I could sit with her.  
She said, “Only if you don’t ask me to stop.”  
I promised I would not.  
We talked for two hours.  
She told me she had Tourette syndrome, not “turrets,” which she said was a common mistake.  
She told me she had been diagnosed at seven years old.  
She told me that her tics changed every few months, like seasons.  
Sometimes she barked.  
Sometimes she cursed.  
Sometimes she just blinked her eyes hard, over and over, until her vision blurred.  
She said the worst part was not the tics themselves.  
The worst part was the way people looked at her, as if she were a puzzle missing a piece.  
I told her she was not missing anything.  
She said, “You don’t know me yet.”  
I said, “I would like to.”  
She gave me her phone number written on a napkin.  
The napkin had a coffee stain shaped like a heart.  
I still have that napkin in a drawer.  
I know that sounds sentimental.  
I do not care.

Section 3
Our first real date was at a park by the river.  
She warned me ahead of time that she might shout or twitch or make sounds like a broken engine.  
I told her I would bring earplugs just in case.  
She laughed, and then she made a sound like a goose being stepped on.  
I did not flinch.  
We sat on a bench and watched the water.  
She told me about her childhood.  
She told me about the kids who mocked her in middle school.  
She told me about the teacher who made her sit in the hallway during tests because her tics distracted others.  
She told me about the first boy she kissed, who later told everyone she was “crazy.”  
I wanted to find that boy and shake him.  
Instead, I held her hand.  
Her hand jerked once, twice, three times.  
I held it tighter.  
She said, “You don’t have to do that.”  
I said, “I know.”  
She said, “Why are you still here?”  
I said, “Because you are the most honest person I have ever met.”  
She said, “That’s a strange reason.”  
I said, “It’s the only one I have.”  
She leaned her head on my shoulder.  
For ten minutes, her body was still.  
Then she shouted, “Tractor!”  
A jogger turned and frowned.  
E

Warmly,

Write a pitch deck for a startup that aims to make a new social network that focuses on the board game society.

---

**Pitch Deck: MeepleHub — The Social Network for Board Gamers**

**Slide 1: Title**
- MeepleHub
- Where Every Game Night Starts
- Tagline: "Roll. Connect. Repeat."

**Slide 2: Problem**
- Board gamers are scattered across generic social platforms (Facebook groups, Discord, Reddit, BGG forums).
- No single place to find local players, schedule game nights, track collections, and discover new games.
- Existing platforms are either too broad (Facebook) or too niche/outdated (BoardGameGeek forums).
- Result: fragmented community, missed connections, and friction for new players.

**Slide 3: Solution**
- MeepleHub: a dedicated social network built for the board game society.
- Core features:
  - Player profiles with game preferences, skill levels, and collection lists.
  - Local matchmaking: find players and groups near you.
  - Event scheduling and RSVP for game nights, conventions, and tournaments.
  - Collection manager with barcode scanning and trade/sell marketplace.
  - Game discovery feed: reviews, session reports, and recommendations.
  - Guilds (communities) for specific games, genres, or regions.

**Slide 4: Why Now**
- Board game industry is booming: $13B+ global market, 10%+ annual growth.
- Post-pandemic surge in analog social activities.
- Gen Z and millennials seek screen-light, in-person social experiences.
- Existing social networks are losing trust and focus; niche networks are winning.

**Slide 5: Market**
- TAM: 100M+ board gamers worldwide (casual + hobbyist).
- SAM: 30M English-speaking active hobbyists who already use digital tools for gaming.
- SOM: 3M early adopters in North America and Europe within 3 years.
- Monetization: freemium subscriptions, marketplace fees, promoted events, game publisher ads.

**Slide 6: Product Demo (Mockups)**
- Home feed: "3 players near you want to play Wingspan this weekend."
- Event page: "Friday Night Catan at Local Cafe — 4/6 spots filled."
- Collection view: "You own 87 games. 12 are tradeable."
- Guild chat: "Azul Strategy Group — 2,400 members."

**Slide 7: Business Model**
- Free tier: basic profile, 1 guild, 5 event RSVPs/month.
- Premium ($4.99/mo): unlimited events, advanced matchmaking, collection analytics, no ads.
- Marketplace: 5% transaction fee on game sales/trades.
- B2B: game publishers pay for targeted demos, surveys, and sponsored tournaments.
- Revenue projection: $1.2M ARR by end of Year 2, $8M by Year 4.

**Slide 8: Traction**
- Waitlist: 12,000 signups from Reddit r/boardgames, BGG, and local meetups.
- 50 beta testers in 3 cities (Austin, Berlin, Toronto).
- 400+ game nights scheduled in beta.
- Partnerships: 3 local game stores, 2 indie publishers.

**Slide 9: Competition**
- BoardGameGeek: database-first, not social; outdated UX.
- Facebook Groups: broad, noisy, no game-specific tools.
- Discord: great for chat, poor for discovery and scheduling.
- Meetup: general events, not board game-specific.
- MeepleHub wins: purpose-built, mobile-first, social graph + game graph combined.

**Slide 10: Go-to-Market**
- Phase 1: Seed with local game stores and meetup organizers (ambassadors).
- Phase 2: Viral loops — invite friends to fill a game table, share session reports.
- Phase 3: Publisher partnerships for sponsored game nights and launch events.
- Phase 4: Expand to conventions (Gen Con, Essen Spiel) with official event tools.

**Slide 11: Team**
- CEO: Former product lead at a social gaming app (5M+ users).
- CTO: Full-stack engineer, built matchmaking systems for sports apps.
- Head of Community: 10-year board game organizer, 20k+ followers on BGG.
- Advisors: Ex-Product at Meetup, board game publisher founder.

**Slide 12: Financials**
- Seed round: $1.5M.
- Use of funds: 50% engineering, 25% community growth, 15% marketing, 10% ops.
- 18-month runway to 100k MAU and $200k MRR.
- Break-even projected in Year 3.

**Slide 13: The Ask**
- Raising $1.5M seed.
- Looking for investors who love games, community, and niche social.
- Join us in building the home for every board gamer.
- Contact: [email protected] | meeplehub.app

**Slide 14: Closing**
- "The board game society deserves its own social network."
- MeepleHub — Roll. Connect. Repeat.

SECTION 1

Harry was a man of simple routines: wake up, make coffee, and argue with his dog, Barnaby, about who owned the sunny spot on the couch. Barnaby was a stout, wheezy bulldog with the face of a retired boxer and the stubbornness of a parking meter. Every morning, Harry would say, “Move it, Barnaby. I pay the rent.” And every morning, Barnaby would fart in response—a sound like a distant tuba—and not move an inch.

SECTION 2

One Tuesday, Harry decided to teach Barnaby to fetch. He tossed a tennis ball across the living room. Barnaby watched it bounce off the TV, then looked at Harry with profound disappointment. Harry tried again. This time, Barnaby slowly stood up, waddled to the ball, and sat on it. “That’s not fetching,” Harry said. Barnaby yawned. Harry then had a brilliant idea: he smeared peanut butter on the ball. Barnaby’s eyes lit up like a slot machine. He inhaled the ball, peanut butter and all, then coughed it back onto the rug, now covered in slobber and shame. Harry stared. “You’re lucky you’re cute.”

SECTION 3

That night, Harry woke to a strange noise. He crept to the kitchen and found Barnaby standing on his hind legs, front paws on the counter, eating an entire stick of butter like a corn cob. “Barnaby!” Harry shouted. The dog froze, butter hanging from his jowls. Then, with the dignity of a king caught stealing a crown, Barnaby dropped the butter, walked to his bed, and farted—long and triumphant. Harry sighed, grabbed a paper towel, and muttered, “Fine. You win the couch tomorrow.” And Barnaby, for the first time ever, wagged his tail.
